name: Yanvalou
desc: The undulating 12/8 Rada invocation rhythm for the serpent-spirit Danbala, the manman drum weaving across a seven-stroke ogan bell. Its three-over-four bell is a Haitian signature timeline.

name: Mayi (Mahi)
desc: A driving 12/8 Rada rhythm named for the Mahi people of Dahomey, faster and more vertical than yanvalou under the same bell. The katabou answers on the offbeat triplet partials.

name: Nago
desc: The martial 12/8 rhythm of the Nago (Yoruba-derived) Ogou warrior spirits, played on Rada drums with proud square accents. It carries the fierce, processional energy of the lwa of iron and war.

name: Ibo
desc: A proud 12/8 rhythm of the Ibo nation lwa, marked by a clipped, dignified bell that drives a slightly faster compound pulse. Danced upright to honour the aloof, aristocratic Ibo spirits.

name: Zepòl
desc: A fast 'shoulder' (zepòl) dance rhythm in 12/8, structurally linked to the Ewe agbekor war music, animating the upper body in jerking shrugs. One of the quickest Rada-family grooves.

name: Petwo
desc: The fiery, binary New-World Petwo rhythm born on Haitian soil, hot and aggressive with cracking whip-like accents for the volatile Petwo lwa. Its straight 4/4 pulse contrasts the ternary Rada family.

name: Kongo
desc: A sensual, swaying binary rhythm of the Kongo nation lwa, favouring 4/4 over the compound Rada meters, with hip-rolling syncopation. Among the few Vodou rhythms played duple rather than in 12/8.

name: Banda
desc: The hip-thrusting Petwo-family rhythm of the Gede death spirits, played for Baron Samedi with lewd, pelvic dance moves. A fast binary groove built on a tresillo-leaning kick.

name: Djouba (Matinik)
desc: The earthy peasant rhythm honouring Kouzen Zaka, the agrarian lwa, performed on Petwo drums with a rustic martinique-derived swing. A binary groove tied to Haiti's farming traditions.

name: Rara
desc: The Lenten street-processional music of Haiti, propelled by tanbou, bamboo vaksen horns and graj scrapers in a marching tresillo. A rowdy carnival cousin of Vodou ceremonial drumming.

name: Méringue
desc: The 19th-century Haitian salon dance rooted in the contredanse and a quintuplet cinquillo cell, ancestor of konpa. Its elegant 2/4 lilt blends European courtliness with Afro-Haitian syncopation.

name: Konpa Dirèk
desc: The smooth modern Haitian dance groove codified by Nemours Jean-Baptiste in 1955, riding a steady 2/4 with a syncopated bass ostinato nudging the beat. The flagship pop rhythm of Francophone Caribbean dancefloors.

name: Rabòday
desc: A contemporary electronic Haitian street style built on Petwo-derived rhythmic cells with punchy digital drums. Carnival energy translated into a modern dancehall-adjacent groove.

name: Bomba Sicá
desc: The most common bomba seis, built on a 3+3+2 tresillo with a steady buleador while the subidor converses with the dancer's piquetes. The signature Afro-Puerto Rican barrel-drum groove.

name: Bomba Yubá
desc: The principal compound-meter (6/8) bomba seis, played at a moderately fast tempo whose ternary feel challenges dancers and drummers alike. The deepest, most African-leaning of the bomba family.

name: Bomba Holandé
desc: One of the fastest bomba styles, traced to Dutch-Caribbean slave cultures of Curaçao, Aruba and St. Croix. A breakneck duple seis driving an urgent tresillo accent.

name: Bomba Cuembé
desc: The second most common bomba seis after sicá, a relaxed mid-tempo groove with sub-styles balancé and gracimá. Its swaying cinquillo-cell feel makes it a favourite for social dancing.

name: Bomba Leró
desc: A slow southern bomba seis from the Ponce region, its name a creole contraction of the French 'le rose' circle dance. A stately 6/8 groove from Puerto Rico's deep south coast.

name: Bomba Gracimá
desc: A cuembé sub-style bomba seis with its own distinct buleador ostinato and dancer-led conversation. A regional variant prized in the bomba canon for its lilting binary push.

name: Bomba Corvé
desc: A bomba seis whose name echoes the French 'corvée' forced-labour origins, danced in compound meter. One of the deep-tradition seises kept alive by Puerto Rico's bomba families.

name: Plena
desc: The 'sung newspaper' of working-class Puerto Rico, played on layered hand-held panderetas: seguidor bass, punteador middle and requinto lead. A 2/4 street rhythm narrating everyday news and gossip.

name: Danza
desc: The refined 19th-century Puerto Rican salon dance whose melodic bass lines elaborate the five-note cinquillo cell over a genteel 2/4. The classical cousin of the island's Afro-Caribbean folk rhythms.

name: Seis
desc: The cuatro-driven jíbaro country music of Puerto Rico's mountain interior, sung in décima verse over a güiro-scraped tresillo. The Spanish-rooted folk counterpart to coastal bomba and plena.

name: Merengue Derecho
desc: The fast straight-ahead Dominican merengue, accordion-led with the tambora's hand-and-stick figure under a relentless güira sixteenth-note saw. The national dance rhythm of the Dominican Republic.

name: Pambiche
desc: The slower, more relaxed 'merengue apambichao' where dancers stay embraced, its tambora syncopation looser than the derecho. A laid-back northern Cibao variant of merengue.

name: Bachata
desc: The romantic Dominican guitar music with its bongo martillo and güira, the fourth-beat accent giving the dance its signature hip-pop. Born in the early 20th century from bolero and Cuban son.

name: Palos (Atabales)
desc: The sacred long-drum (atabales) music of Dominican folk-Catholic saint festivals and cofradías, deeply Afro-Dominican and largely in compound meter. The spiritual ceremonial drumming of the DR.

name: Gagá
desc: The Dominican Holy-Week processional music of the bateyes, the cross-border cousin of Haitian rara with bamboo trumpets and marching drums. A defiant Afro-Dominican Lenten street rhythm.

name: Salve
desc: The hybrid sacred-secular song-form sung to the Virgin in Dominican folk-Catholic vigils, its Africanized variants driven by panderos and balsié in compound time. The most ubiquitous Dominican religious rhythm.

name: Pri-Prí
desc: The southern Dominican 'merengue palo echao' from the Villa Mella region, an accordion-and-balsié folk groove leaning on a tresillo kick. A rootsy rural cousin of mainstream merengue.

name: Sarandunga
desc: The devotional drum-and-dance tradition of Baní honouring San Juan Bautista, played on three small tamboras and a güira in lively compound meter. A tightly localized Afro-Dominican festival rhythm.

name: Mento
desc: Jamaica's rural acoustic precursor to ska, with banjo, rhumba box and a relaxed afterbeat lilt that emphasizes the final beat of the bar. The folk root from which all later Jamaican pop grew.

name: Nyabinghi
desc: The Rastafari hand-drumming heartbeat in 4/4: the thunder bass open on beat 1 and damped on beat 3, the funde holding the offbeat one-two, the repeater improvising. The sacred ancestor of reggae's one-drop.

name: Ska
desc: The bouncy early-1960s Jamaican beat with its choppy guitar skank on the offbeats and a walking bass, born of mento meeting American R&B. The first great Jamaican pop rhythm.

name: Rocksteady
desc: The slowed-down, soul-tinged 1966 successor to ska, with a relaxed backbeat, sparser bass and the skank still riding the offbeats. The bridge from ska to roots reggae.

name: Reggae One Drop
desc: The classic roots-reggae feel: kick and rim-shot landing together on beat 3 with beat 1 left empty, the skank hats barking on every offbeat. The defining groove of Bob Marley-era reggae.

name: Reggae Rockers
desc: The driving Sly-Dunbar 1970s rockers feel, adding a kick on beat 1 to the one-drop for a more insistent, four-square push. A heavier alternative to the one-drop.

name: Reggae Steppers
desc: The militant 'steppers' feel with a four-on-the-floor kick driving the riddim relentlessly forward under an offbeat skank. The most propulsive of the roots-reggae drum styles.

name: Dub
desc: King Tubby and Lee Perry's studio art-form: a spacious one-drop drenched in reverb and tape delay, with instruments dropping in and out and open-hat splashes. Reggae remixed into cavernous soundscape.

name: Dancehall (Sleng Teng)
desc: The 1985 digital riddim from a Casiotone MT-40 'rock' preset that birthed dancehall, built on a dotted, lurching shape rather than a 2-and-4 backbeat. The single most versioned riddim in Jamaican history.

name: Ragga
desc: The fully digital branch of dancehall foregrounding synthesized sub-bass, drum-machine riddims and rapid-fire patois toasting. The mid-1980s electronic evolution of Jamaican sound-system music.

name: Calypso
desc: The lilting Trinidadian carnival song-form, ancestor of soca, built on a son-clave-leaning kick and a bright backbeat. The voice of social commentary and calypsonian wit.

name: Soca
desc: Lord Shorty's 1970s 'soul of calypso' fusion: a four-on-the-floor kick under a syncopated snare, hats playing three sixteenths and opening on the fourth. The driving engine of modern Carnival.

name: Chutney Soca
desc: The Indo-Caribbean fusion of dholak-and-dhantal beats with the soca engine, born of Trinidad's Bhojpuri heritage. A whirling sixteenth-note dance rhythm bridging India and the Caribbean.

name: Parang
desc: Trinidad's Spanish-language Christmas serenading music from Paramin and Lopinot, rooted in Venezuelan aguinaldo with cuatro, maracas and a 6/8 hemiola feel. The festive parranda tradition of the hills.

name: Steelpan (Engine Room)
desc: The driving 'engine room' percussion section of a Carnival steelband, with iron, scratchers and brake-drums laying down a relentless soca-calypso pulse beneath the pans. The rhythmic heart of pan-on-the-road.

name: Punta
desc: The most popular Garifuna rhythm, a fast hip-swivelling dance with the segunda bass drum holding steady while the primero improvises faster fills. The signature beat of the Central American Garinagu.

name: Paranda
desc: The slower, soulful Garifuna song-form sung by male paranderos over acoustic guitar and gentle drums, telling stories of love and struggle. The bluesy, contemplative side of Garifuna music.

name: Hunguhungu
desc: A Garifuna circle dance in a swaying three-beat compound meter, often combined with punta in ceremony. Its rolling 6/8 lilt accompanies communal ritual gatherings.

name: Chumba
desc: A solo Garifuna mime-dance in a three-beat rhythm, frequently paired with hunguhungu, in which the dancer playfully interprets the song's story. A theatrical, individual showcase within the Garifuna repertoire.

name: Junkanoo
desc: The explosive Bahamian carnival parade music of goatskin goombay drums, cowbells, whistles and brass, with cowbells ringing on the offbeats over a marching kick. The riotous street pulse of Boxing Day and New Year.

name: Rake-and-Scrape
desc: The Bahamian folk groove driven by a carpenter's saw scraped with a screwdriver, a goombay drum and accordion, accompanying the quadrille and heel-toe polka. The rural Family-Islands dance rhythm.

name: Léwòz
desc: The most complex of the seven gwoka rhythms, a moderate-tempo incantation groove tied to the 18th-century maroon resistance societies. The intense centerpiece of the Guadeloupean léwòz gathering.

name: Kaladja
desc: The slow, sorrowful gwoka rhythm of heartbreak and the struggle in love, swaying in a heavy compound feel. The most plaintive of the seven Guadeloupean rhythms.

name: Toumblak
desc: The fast, joyous gwoka rhythm of love, fertility and sensuality, the most widely known of the seven with a bouncing duple drive. The crowd-pleasing celebratory groove of gwoka.

name: Graj
desc: A steady work-rhythm of gwoka whose movements mime the grating of cassava into flour, slower than toumblak. The agricultural labour song of Guadeloupe's countryside.

name: Woulé
desc: The slow, deep gwoka 'creole waltz' in three time, danced to gently mock the planters' European ballroom steps. The graceful ternary rhythm of the seven.

name: Padjabèl
desc: A humorous work-dance of gwoka recalling the jerking movements of sugarcane cutting and women's liberation from bondage. A spirited rhythm of plantation memory and pride.

name: Mendé
desc: The last gwoka rhythm to arrive, brought by post-abolition Congo contract workers, a fast carnival-and-parade groove of collective celebration. The most outward-facing, festive rhythm of the seven.

name: Bélé
desc: The Martinican drum-and-dance tradition in which the tibwa sticks beat the cinquillo on bamboo while the tambour bélé marks the accents and improvises. The deep Afro-Creole root of Martinican music.

name: Biguine
desc: The early-20th-century Martinican dance blending bélé drumming with European ballroom and clarinet-led ensembles, a syncopated 2/4 that conquered 1930s Paris. The elegant urban face of Antillean music.

name: Zouk
desc: The 1980s Kassav'-led Antillean pop fusion of gwoka, bélé and biguine vidé, with the tibwa simplified to an almost-constant 3+3+2 motive on rimshots. The international dance sound of the French Caribbean.
